entries.name: Ethiopian Christianity — Gondar to the Zemene Mesafint
entries.informalName: The Church under the Gondar Kings
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). It fills the two centuries between the end of the Jesuit mission and the rise of Tewodros II. Its window runs from 1650 to 1855. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Almost every text read here is an outsider's. Ludolf wrote in 1682, Bruce in 1790 and Gobat in 1834. A Catholic encyclopedia of 1907 adds the missions' side. The royal chronicles in Ge'ez are the church's own court voice, but the copies found could not be opened. The voices of monks and lay people are thin.
entries.floorNote: No question. It is the same church as the entries on either side of it. No dated statement of its own from these years was read.
entries.relationsSummary: It carries on the church of the entry before it, which ends with the Jesuits gone. It carries into the church of Tewodros II. The abun came from the Coptic church in Egypt, as the Coptic entry of these years also shows.
entries.why: After the Jesuits left, Ethiopia gave up dealings with Europe. The church went on under its abun, who came from Egypt. Its monks quarreled, and in troubled times their chiefs held more weight than the abun did.
entries.teaser: Ethiopia, 1650 to 1855 — a church that turned from Europe after the Jesuits left. It went on under its abuns, its monks and its councils.
entries.longDescription:
By 1650 the Jesuits were gone. Hiob Ludolf, writing in 1682, says that Fasilides drove them out of all his lands, together with their patriarch. Ludolf adds that Europeans knew little more of the emperor after that, because he would have no more dealings with them.

The head of the church was the abun, and he came from Egypt. James Bruce, who was in Ethiopia in the early 1770s, calls him a Coptic monk raised in the desert of St Macarius. Bruce says people looked on the abun as the patriarch of their church, and that they knew little of the Coptic patriarch of Alexandria. He adds that the abun seldom understood the language of the country.

The monks held great weight. Bruce says the Itchege, the chief of the monks of Debra Libanos, mattered more than the abun in troubled times. He names the monks of Gojam, who followed St Eustathius, as the low church of Ethiopia, and says they leaned toward turmoil in matters of religion. Bruce was an outside witness. He wrote decades after some of the events he tells.

Councils of clergy met when a new king took the throne or a new abun came from Egypt. Bruce tells of one in the reign of David. The head of the monks of Debra Libanos brought a complaint against three Catholic priests and their Ethiopian interpreter, also named Abba Gregorius. The council asked whether they accepted the Council of Chalcedon and the authority of Pope Leo. They said that they did, and the crowd cried out, "Stone them." The missionaries were dragged to a place behind the church of Abbo and stoned to death.

The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1907 also tells of three missionaries stoned in a public square at Gondar. It dates this to 1752. No other source read here gives that date.

The article also says that in 1846 Rome made Abyssinia a vicariate. Rome gave it to the Lazarists. It says one of them, Justin de Jacobis, stirred the jealousy of the clergy. These accounts are Catholic. They speak for the missionaries.

The Church Missionary Society had long turned its eyes toward Ethiopia. It sent Samuel Gobat and Christian Kugler into Egypt in 1826 to seek a way in. On 26 February 1830 Gobat left Adigrate, in Tigray, and set out for Gondar.

Gobat's journal also shows how the church settled a quarrel in Tigray. A letter of Kugler's tells that Girgis and the chief priest of Tigray, Guebra Mariam, came from Cairo. They brought the decision of the Coptic patriarch on the priests' quarrels. One priest, Guebra Messih, held that Christ had three births. On 28 September the dispute was settled in the presence of the Tigray ruler Sebagadis.

The next entry says that for a century before 1855 the emperors were only figureheads, while regional lords ruled. No source read for this entry tells of those years.
voices: Hiob Ludolf — a German scholar who wrote his history of Ethiopia in 1682 from the words of an Ethiopian, Abba Gregorius
James Bruce — a Scottish traveler at Gondar in the early 1770s, an outside witness
Samuel Gobat — the Church Missionary Society man whose journal of three years in Abyssinia came out in 1834
The Ethiopian clergy of these years speak only through outsiders: the council that tried the Catholic priests, and the priests of Tigray in Gobat's journal
entries.legacy:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church of today is the same church, on the usual reading. The church of the next window still took its abun from Egypt.

Much of these two centuries is still untold here. The royal chronicles and the monks' own words are not yet read.

livingEvidence.basis: The same church as the entries on either side of it. It reaches today through the entry on modern Ethiopian and Eritrean Christianity, which holds the dated evidence. All of that evidence is graded CR (Contemporary-Reported), and none of it was read for this record.

entries.name: The Coptic Church under the Ottomans: the Patriarchate and the Archons
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its window runs from 1517, the Ottoman conquest, to 1854, where the entry on the Coptic revival begins. It starts in the era before the one it sits in. The years 1300 to 1517 are not yet told in any entry.
entries.sourcing: Moderate, and mostly from outsiders. Volney wrote in the 1780s and Lane in the 1830s. Butcher's study of 1897 tells the church's history. The Arabic History of the Patriarchs and the archons' own letters and deeds are not in the Library.
entries.floorNote: No question. It is the same church as the entries before and after it, which hold the ancient miaphysite confession. No dated statement of its own from these centuries was read.
entries.relationsSummary: It is the same Coptic church that the entries before and after it follow. Its patriarchs run in one numbered line through the Ottoman conquest of 1517. Its patriarch's rulings reached Ethiopia, and Rome set up a Catholic line among the Copts in 1741.
entries.why: Under Ottoman rule the Copts were a minority. Lay notables kept the land books and the money. One of them, Ibrahim al-Jawhari, gave land and money to restore churches and monasteries. The patriarch judged small cases.
entries.teaser: Egypt, 1517 to 1854 — a church under Ottoman rule, led by its patriarchs and by lay notables. They kept the government's books and paid for its churches.
entries.longDescription:
In 1517 the Ottomans took Egypt. A list of the Coptic patriarchs, compiled by E. A. Wallis Budge and printed in 1928, runs on without a break through that year. It shows John XIII in office to 1524, and Gabriel VII from 1526 to 1569.

Volney traveled in Egypt and Syria from 1783 to 1785. He says the Copts had become the keepers of the registers of the lands and tribes. He says that at Cairo they served as the government's stewards, secretaries and tax collectors. He writes that the Turks they served despised them, and the peasants they pressed hated them. Volney was no friend of the Copts.

These lay leaders are called archons. One was Ibrahim al-Jawhari, chief clerk of the finance office. Butcher says he was so well liked by Muslim and Christian that he escaped a persecution under Hassan Pasha in the 1780s. Through his influence the churches and monasteries could be restored, and he gave much land and money to the church.

Edward Lane wrote his account of Egypt in the years 1833 to 1835. He reckoned the Copts at about 150,000. He writes that the Coptic patriarch judged small cases among his people in Cairo.

Rome built a Catholic line among the Copts. In 1741 the pope made a Copt named Athanasius a metropolitan.

He lived in Jerusalem. Butcher calls him the first with real power in Egypt. He named a priest as his vicar there. Butcher wrote in 1897 and did not favor Rome's claim.

The patriarch also sent the abun to Ethiopia. A decision of his reached Tigray, as Gobat's journal shows.
voices: Ibrahim al-Jawhari — chief clerk of the finance office, known only through Butcher's account
Athanasius — a Copt of Jerusalem, made the first Catholic metropolitan with real power in Egypt in 1741
The Coptic patriarchs — a numbered line in Budge's list, with none speaking here in his own words
entries.legacy:
The Coptic Orthodox Church of today is the same church, on the usual reading. The next entry begins with the patriarch Cyril IV in 1854.

Much of these centuries is still untold here. The Arabic History of the Patriarchs is not yet in the Library.

livingEvidence.basis: The same church, carried into the next entry and on to the twentieth-century revival. It reaches today through the entry on the Coptic monastic and Sunday-school revival, which holds the dated evidence. That evidence is graded CR (Contemporary-Reported). Only one item of it was read for this record: a study of Habib Girgis, published in 2017.

entries.name: Kongo Christianity after 1650
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) for about 1650 to 1720, where Capuchin eyewitnesses are in the Library. Later years rest on thinner sources, and the entry says so. Its window runs from 1650 to 1881. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Good for the first half and thin for the middle. Two Capuchins are read here: Carli in 1671 and Cavazzi in 1687. Two more, Merolla and Zucchelli, are in the Library but were not read for this entry. Almost every text is a missionary's. Bentley, a Baptist writing in 1900, covers the end. Kongolese letters of the period are not in the Library.
entries.floorNote: No question. It is the Catholic Church in Kongo, as in the entry before it.
entries.relationsSummary: It carries on the church of King Afonso I, which the entry before it follows to 1650. The Antonian movement of 1704 to 1706 falls inside it. A Baptist station came to San Salvador in 1879 and Portuguese priests in 1881.
entries.why: Kongo had been Christian for well over a century in 1650. Capuchin friars came to serve it. Their own books show baptized adults and children brought for baptism, and places that priests rarely reached.
entries.teaser: The Kingdom of Kongo, 1650 to 1881 — a Christian people served by Capuchin friars. Priests were few in many places. Baptists and Portuguese priests came to the old capital in 1879 and 1881.
entries.longDescription:
In the late 1660s two Capuchin friars, Dionigi Carli and Michelangelo Guattini, served in Bamba, in Kongo. Carli's book came out in 1671. He writes that a headman sent word through the village to bring the children for baptism, because the adults were all baptized. The people called the friar "Ngamga," and Carli adds that they put a word after it to honor him.

Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi was a Capuchin. He printed his history of Kongo, Matamba and Angola in 1687. He writes that priests rarely came to remote places to keep the law of Christ in force. The people there still took pride in it.

Cavazzi tells of the queen Njinga, whom he calls queen of the Jaga. He says she turned her back on the true law and joined the Jaga. He says that for twenty-eight years she followed a way of life he calls the most beastly of all. Her later return to the church is not shown in the text read here.

The Antonian movement of Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita, from 1704 to 1706, falls inside this window. John Thornton's study of 1998 treats it, and how far it grew from the older church rests on that one study.

Almost nothing was read for the years from about 1720 to 1879. How the church lived then waits on sources not yet read.

Bentley's list dates the Baptist station at San Salvador to 1879. The Portuguese priests there first came in 1881. Bentley judged from what he heard that the people were about evenly split between the priests and the Baptists.

entries.name: The Dutch Reformed Church at the Cape
entries.informalName: The Settlers' Church of the Cape
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its window runs from the settlers' landing in 1652 to 1906. It is the first entry for the settlers' church in South Africa. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Moderate. The main source read is John McCarter's history of 1869, a friendly account. Synod acts, Andrew Murray's own works and Dutch and Afrikaans church histories were not read. The voices of slaves and Khoikhoi members are thin.
entries.floorNote: No question. McCarter lists its standards as the Heidelberg Catechism, the Belgic Confession and the Canons of Dort.
entries.relationsSummary: Its standards came from the Netherlands, among them the Canons of Dort. It began as the Company's church at Table Bay. The Trek of the 1830s took many of its people inland, and new churches grew beyond the colony.
entries.why: The Dutch East India Company's settlers landed at Table Bay in 1652. Slaves were baptized in the church from the 1660s. It held its first synod in 1824, under the eye of the government. It was tested by the Trek and by the Burgers case in the civil court.
entries.teaser: South Africa, 1652 to 1906 — the settlers' church of the Cape, from slave baptisms at Table Bay to the synod of 1824 and the courtroom of 1865.
entries.longDescription:
On 6 April 1652 three Dutch ships dropped anchor in Table Bay with a small band of settlers. John McCarter, writing in 1869, says the Company that sent them did not mean to found a colony in the modern sense.

McCarter names van Arckel as the first minister. On his arrival in 1665 he baptized eight children, on their owners' promise to bring them up in the fear of the Lord. The church books record the baptisms of 1,121 slave children and forty-six adults between 1665 and 1731.

McCarter reports a rule of 1683 that a slave received into the church was free at once, and says many were freed this way. He names no source for the rule, and this entry has not checked it.

In 1688, McCarter says, about 150 French refugees came to the Cape. He says that by 1869 their descendants numbered at least 200,000.

The church held its first synod in 1824. By then it had thirteen congregations.

The government sent two men to sit in. Every decision went to the governor to approve.

Some ministers wanted a book of hymns sung beside the Psalms, and part of the people opposed it. McCarter says a group called the Doppers formed a kind of sect inside the church, and has since become a separate body.

McCarter says a frontier war in 1835 brought long-growing discontent to a crisis, and many farmers decided to leave the colony. In the Transvaal, he counts three religious parties.

In the 1860s the church's commission suspended a minister, T. F. Burgers. His case came before the Supreme Court of the Cape on 26 May 1865. Andrew Murray the younger was summoned as moderator of the synod.

This entry does not yet tell how the church came to hold separate churches by race. That story waits on sources not yet read.

entries.name: Southern African Mission Churches
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) as an entry of its own. It gathers several mission societies' churches. Its window runs from 1737 to 1906. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Good for the mission side and thin for the African side. Philip, Casalis and Chalmers all wrote as missionaries or as their friends. Tiyo Soga's letter reaches us only through Chalmers, and Ntsikana's hymn is not in the Library.
entries.floorNote: No question for the mainline mission churches named here. No dated statement of each sending church was read.
entries.relationsSummary: Missionaries of four societies worked here. This entry follows Schmidt's Moravian mission of 1737. It also follows the Xhosa and Sotho Christians. The settlers' Dutch Reformed Church is told in its own entry.
entries.why: The first Protestant mission in South Africa began with Georg Schmidt among the Khoikhoi in 1737. It was dropped for nearly fifty years and then taken up again. Xhosa Christians such as Ntsikana and Tiyo Soga then took their place beside the missionaries, and the Paris mission came to the Sotho.
entries.teaser: Southern Africa, 1737 to 1906. Mission churches grew among the Khoikhoi, the Xhosa and the Sotho.
entries.longDescription:
McCarter calls the Moravians' work at the Cape the earliest South African mission. Georg Schmidt sailed for the Cape in 1737 and by September lived at Baviaans Kloof, now Genadendal. He could not learn the Khoikhoi language and spoke through an interpreter. At the end of 1740 he wrote that his congregation had thirty-two people, and that fifteen of them read the New Testament in Dutch. In 1742, McCarter says, he baptized the first of them.

The Moravians' own account of 1771 says the brethren lived five years there. They opened a school. They baptized seven adults. Then "certain circumstances" ended the mission.

McCarter says the work lapsed for nearly fifty years. Then three Germans took it up again.

John Philip wrote in 1828 about Dr Vanderkemp. Philip says he began his work among people who had risen against the farmers.

He says the other London mission stations in the colony grew out of Bethelsdorp. Others, he says, were formed from the last Khoikhoi still living in their old way.

Eugène Casalis was a missionary of the Paris Evangelical mission. He wrote of his first meeting with Moshoeshoe, whom he calls Moshesh, in 1833. He says the first days went to explaining why the missionaries had come. He writes that the people had long called their chief the Chief of the Mountain.

John Chalmers wrote of Ntsikana in 1877. Ntsikana was the head man of a village. After the missionary Williams died, Chalmers says, Ntsikana kept up religious services with his people. Before his death, about the beginning of 1821, he told them to move to the station on the Gwali.

Chalmers also tells of Tiyo Soga, whom he calls the first ordained preacher of his race. On 23 July 1861 Soga wrote that he opened the service for the first stone of the Mgwali mission church with the great hymn of Ntsikana. Chalmers says the missionaries named in this part of his book were, with one exception, sent by the Glasgow Missionary Society.

Ntsikana's hymn is not yet in the Library, and Soga's own letters reach us only through Chalmers.

set.longDescription:
For a century Ethiopia's emperors had been figureheads while regional lords ruled. Then in 1855 a soldier from the provinces took the throne as Tewodros II. He set out to remake the empire, and its church too. He seized church lands and tried to bring the clergy under his hand. His quarrel with Britain ended in 1868, when a British army stormed Magdala and he took his own life. Yohannes IV took the throne a few years later. He settled an argument that had split Ethiopian scholars for two centuries. At the Council of Boru Meda in 1878 he ruled for the Tewahedo teaching on how God and man are united in Christ. He then made it the one teaching of the empire. Menelik II did what no other African ruler managed in that century. At Adwa in 1896 he crushed an invading Italian army and kept his country free. Ethiopia entered the twentieth century as an ancient Christian state that had never been ruled by Europeans. Its church still took its head, the abun, from the Coptic patriarch in Egypt.

Missionaries kept coming. Donald Crummey wrote about them in a study of the missions from 1830 to 1868. It is called Priests and Politicians.

A Catholic source of 1907 says Tewodros made Catholics suffer. It says Yohannes brought them twenty years of trouble.

It says Menelik, crowned in March 1889, restored calm to the missions. This is a Catholic account, not the church's own.
